1.1 Addressing safety of self, others 
and the environment 
You should be able to: 
¢ recognize and address relevant safety, ethical and environmental issues in an investigation. 
Lab safety is an essential attribute of the learner profile. In conducting 
experimental work, you must take responsibility for your actions and their 
consequences. 
Accident prevention is the cornerstone of lab safety. It includes wearing 
personal protective equipment (PPE), conducting risk assessments, putting Nature of science 
the correct control measures in place and reducing risks by using safer alternatives. Accident prevention and waste 
prevention are two of the twelve 
Common PPE includes safety goggles, lab coats and protective gloves. principles of green chemistry. 
Certain experiments might require extra PPE, such as face shields, respirators 
and safety shoes. 
Before carrying out any experiment, a risk assessment must be completed. Risk 
assessments cover identification of hazards, ways of minimizing the risks and 
emergency measures that must be taken if something goes wrong. 
* Ahazard is a substance or activity that has the potential to cause 
harm (e.g. a toxic chemical or hot crucible). 
* Riskis the likelihood and severity of harm to the researcher, other lab 
users and the environment (e.g. poisoning by the toxic chemical or 
getting burned by the hot crucible). 
¢ A control measure is what must be done to minimize the risk 
(e.g. wear PPE, use tongs to pick up the hot crucible) and deal with 
accidents (e.g. have a first-aid kit and an emergency phone in the 
laboratory). 
Safety must be kept in mind before, during and after the experiment. To 
minimize the risks and protect the environment, the smallest possible 
quantities of chemicals must be used, and the waste must be disposed of in 
accordance with local rules and policies. When practical and safe, solvents 
and unreacted chemicals should be recovered and reused. The use of energy 
and water must also be minimized.

Systematic errors can be minimized, but not eliminated, by making changes to 
the experimental methodology, which include calibration, thermal insulation 
and thorough checks of the equipment. If a particular systematic error can be

The quality of measurement is also characterized by validity, which shows 
whether the measurement results make sense and reflect the actual parameter 
being measured, and reliability, which shows whether the results are 
reproducible when the measurement is repeated under the same conditions. 
Assessment tip 
Validity and reliability are independent characteristics. For example, an 
attempt to measure temperature using a pH probe instead of thermometer 
might produce results that will be reliable (consistent) but invalid, as they 
will have no relation to the actual temperature of the sample. 
In turn, reliability is characterized by repeatability (the agreement of results 
when trials are repeated by the same researcher using the same instrument 
and the same sample) and reproducibility (the consistency of results obtained 
by different people using different instruments and reagent sources). In some 
cases, a measurement must be repeated until the values become concordant =

Time 
Time in chemical experiments is commonly measured using a stopwatch or a 
digital device that is triggered automatically by a certain event, such as loading 
a sample into an instrument. The precision of a typical stopwatch (0.075s) is 
higher than the time delay caused by the experimenter’s reaction time (up to 
0.55), which must be taken into account when recording and processing time￾related data, such as reaction rates (Reactivity 2.2). 
Time intervals greater than one hour can be measured using any watch or 
clock, as a precision of 1 s or even 1 minute is sufficient for most long-running 
experiments. 
Temperature 
Temperature is measured by digital or analogue thermometers. The required 
accuracy and precision of a temperature measurement depend on the context 
of the experiment. Continuous monitoring of temperature can be achieved by 
connecting a temperature probe to a data logger or computer. 
Length 
Length can be measured using a ruler or, if a higher precision is required, a 
calliper. Rulers are analogue devices, so the resolution of their scale affects the 
number of significant figures in the measurement (figure 7). The last significant 
figure in a length measurement can never be obtained with certainty but only 
estimated, depending on the position of the measured object between two 
adjacent scale divisions.

Electric current, conductivity and potential difference 
Electric current is measured in amperes (A) using an ammeter, which is 
connected in series with the analysed solution (flgure 10). To test a solid 
sample, the electrodes are replaced with metal clamps that are attached 
directly to the opposite ends of the sample. In a series connection, the 
electric current flowing through all components is identical, so the ammeter 
can be placed anywhere in the circuit. A good ammeter must have very low 
electrical resistance to ensure that the measured current is not limited by the 
ammeter itself.

1.3 Applying techniques 
You should be able to: 
v’ show awareness of the purpose and practice of preparing a standard solution, carrying out dilutions, 
drying to constant mass, distillation and reflux, paper or thin layer chromatography, separation of mixtures, 
calorimetry, acid-base and redox titrations, electrochemical cells, colorimetry or spectrophotometry, 
physical and digital molecular modelling, recrystallization, and melting point determination. 
Preparation of standard solutions 
A standard solution is a solution of areactant, such as an acid or a base, with 
known concentration. The preparation of astandard solution involves the 
following steps (figure 12): 
* weigh the solid or liquid sample in a clean and dry beaker using an 
analytical balance 
* dissolve the sample by adding a small volume of deionized water to the 
beaker and stirring the mixture with a glass rod 
* transfer the solution to a volumetric flask using a glass funnel 
* rinse the beaker, glass rod and funnel three times with deionized water and 
add the water to the volumetric flask 
* fill the flask with deionized water to the graduation mark 
* stopper the flask and turn it over at least ten times to produce a uniform 
solution 
* transfer the solution to a reagent bottle with a descriptive label.

1.3 Applying techniques 
Drying solid samples 
Solid samples often contain adsorbed water, so they must be dried to constant 
mass as follows: 
* place an evaporating dish on an analytical balance and press the “Tare” button 
¢ place the sample into the dish and record the initial mass 
s transfer the dish to a hot oven and keep it there for a certain time 
* using tongs, transfer the hot dish to a desiccator containing a drying agent, 
such as solid anhydrous calcium chloride or phosphorus(V) oxide 
* close the lid of the desiccator and allow the sample to cool down 
¢ place the dish with the sample on the analytical balance and record the 
new mass 
* repeat the sequence of drying, cooling and weighing until at least two 
concordant results are obtained. 
The temperature of the oven must be sufficient for complete removal of 
water from the sample but it must not be too high, otherwise the sample 
may decompose. The dried sample must be kept in the desiccator or used 
immediately after the last weighing. Upon prolonged contact with air, the sample 
will re-adsorb moisture, so the drying procedure will have to be repeated. 
Distillation and heating under reflux 
Mixtures of two or more liquids can be separated by fractional distillation 
(figure 13). When a mixture of liquids is heated, the most volatile component 
evaporates first, passes through the fractionating column and enters the 
condenser, where it turns back to liquid and flows into the receiver flask. 
Less volatile liquids remain in the flask until the first component (fraction) has 
evaporated completely. After that, the temperature of the mixture rises, so the 
remaining liquids evaporate one by one, according to their boiling points. Thus, 
each component of the mixture can be collected separately by replacing the 
receiver between fractions. The fractionating column is a long tube filled with 
glass beads, which increase the surface area and facilitate the separation through 
multiple cycles of evaporation and condensation. During the distillation, the 
most volatile component moves up the column while less volatile components 
condense on the glass beads and drip back into the distillation flask.

Simple distillation is similar to fractional distillation except that it does not 
require a fractionating column. Simple distillation can be used for separating a 
volatile liquid from non-volatile liquid or solid impurities. 
Heating under reflux is a technigue that permits volatile liquids to be treated 
with other reactants at their boiling point for long periods of time (figure 14). 
When the reaction mixture is heated in a flask fitted with a reflux condenser, the 
vapour of the volatile liquid rises into the condenser, turns into liquid and drips 
back into the flask. 
Heating under reflux is used in the preparation of carboxylic acids from 
alcohols (Reactivity 3.2). The volatile aldehyde is continuously returned 
to the reaction flask until its oxidation is complete. 
Assessment tip 
In both distillation and reflux, the smooth boiling of the mixture is achieved 
by using anti-bumping granules (figures 13 and 14). This is an important 
safety measure because it greatly reduces the chance of the mixture 
“bumping” and overflowing the condenser, which can potentially cause 
spillage and fire. 
Chromatography 
Chromatography is a collective term for several analytical technigues in which 
a mixture is separated into its components according to their relative affinities 
to the mobile and stationary phases. In paper chromatography (figure 15), 
the stationary phase is a rectangular piece of chromatographic paper, and 
the mobile phase is an organic solvent. In thin-layer chromatography (TLC), 
the paper is replaced with a metal or glass plate covered with a thin layer of 
silica (Si0,).

In both paper chromatography and TLC, the analysed mixture is spotted on 
the start line, and the paper or TLC plate is dipped into the solvent. Polar 
substances have greater affinity for the stationary phase, so their molecules 
spend most of the time being adsorbed on the paper or silica. In contrast, 
non-polar substances are more soluble in the mobile phase, so their molecules 
spend more time in the solvent. Adsorbed molecules remain stationary while

dissolved molecules move along with the solvent. Therefore, the components 
of the mixture are separated according to their polarity: the lower the polarity 
of the component, the faster it moves along the paper or TLC plate. 
When the separation is complete, the paper or plate is removed from the 
beaker, the position of the solvent front is marked with a pencil, and the 
chromatogram is allowed to dry. The spots of separated components are 
revealed using UV light or a locating reagent, such as iodine or ninhydrin. 
Relative positions of the spots are characterized by their retardation factors, R,.

Each substance has a specific R, value for a given stationary phase, solvent 
and temperature, so the components in a mixture can be identified using 
standard samples or literature data. 
Separation of mixtures 
Apart from chromatography, mixtures can be separated using various 
technigues, which include filtration, extraction, crystallization and distillation 
(see table 1in Structure 1.1). 
Gravity filtration is used to separate solids from liquids: when a mixture is 
poured onto a filter, the liquid passes through and drips into a flask while the 
solid remains on the filter (figure 16). After washing and drying, the solid is 
collected from the filter. 
Vacuum filtration is similar to gravity filtration except that the process is 
accelerated by applying vacuum to the flask (figure 17). 
Extraction is a separation method based on a difference in solubility. In the 
simplest case, a solid mixture is treated with a solvent that dissolves only 
one component. The remaining components are filtered off and the solvent 
is evaporated, leaving the soluble component behind. Then the process is 
repeated using different solvents until all components are separated. 
Liquid-liquid extraction involves two immiscible solvents with different 
polarities, such as water and hexane. A mixture is added to the solvents and 
shaken vigorously. Polar components dissolve in the polar solvent while non￾polar components pass into the non-polar solvent. After a while, the resulting 
solutions form two layers, which are collected in different beakers using a 
separating funnel (figure 18). Each solution is evaporated, leaving the dissolved 
components of the mixture behind. For complex mixtures, this process can 
be repeated several times using different solvents until all components are 
isolated as individual compounds.

Crystallization is used to isolate a pure solid component from a solution. In the 
simplest case, most of the solvent is distilled off, and the remaining solution 
is cooled down slowly to allow crystals to form. The crystals are isolated 
by filtration, washed with a small quantity of cold solvent and dried to a 
constant mass. 
Recrystallization is a similar technigue that is used to purify a solid sample 
(figure 19). First, the sample is dissolved in a hot solvent, then the hot solution 
is filtered quickly to remove insoluble impurities and allowed to cool down 
slowly. The pure solid crystallizes while soluble impurities remain in the 
solution. The crystals are then filtered, washed and dried as described earlier.

Titration 
Titration is an analytical method used to determine the unknown concentration 
of asubstance (analyte) in solution. In a typical titration experiment, a 
carefully measured volume (V], known as aliguot) of the analysed solution 
is placed in a conical flask, and a solution of a suitable reactant (titrant) with 
known concentration (Cz) is added dropwise from a burette until all analyte 
is consumed (figure 22). The titrant volume (V) used in the experiment is 
recorded, and the titration is repeated until at least two concordant V, values 
(typically within £0.05 cm?) are obtained. If the analyte and titrant react in a 
1:1 ratio, the unknown concentration of the analyte (cl) is determined as follows:

The titrant chosen for a titration must react with the analyte quickly and 
quantitatively. In acid-base titrations, acids are titrated with bases, and bases 
with acids. The moment of complete neutralization, known as the equivalence 
point, can be detected visually using an acid-base indicator (Reactivity 3.1 
AHL), which is added to the analyte before the titration. Alternatively, the 
equivalence point can be determined more accurately using a pH probe (see 
figure 9). 
Redox titrations are similar to acid-base titrations except that the analyte 
and titrant participate in a redox reaction instead of neutralization. Reducing 
analytes are titrated with oxidizing agents, and oxidizing analytes with 
reducing agents. The equivalence point in a redox titration can be detected 
using a redox indicator that changes colour when the analyte is used up 
completely. Many redox titrations are self-indicating because either the analyte 
or titrant, or both, change colour in the course of the reaction. 
Electrochemical cells 
Electrochemical cells interconvert chemical energy and electrical energy. Voltaic 
(galvanic) cells use the chemical energy of spontaneous redox reactions to 
generate electricity whereas electrolytic cells use externally supplied electrical 
energy to drive forward non-spontaneous redox reactions. All types of cells 
contain electrodes and electrolytes. In addition, voltaic cells usually contain a 
salt bridge that allows ions to move between the electrolytes of the two half-cells 
whereas electrolytic cells require a power source. External wiring completes the 
circuit by allowing the electrons to move between the electrodes.

Sensors 
Sensors, such as digital thermometers and pH probes, are used to measure 
physical properties and transmit the results to other devices for processing. 
Maodern digital sensors are more compact, accurate and precise than 
traditional analogue devices. In addition, digital sensors can be connected to 
data loggers that collect and save measurement results at regular intervals. 
Like any scientific instruments, sensors require regular checks and calibration. 
This is particularly important forsensors that measure a certain property 
continuously, as any malfunction or loss of accuracy in this type of equipment can 
remain unnoticed for a long time and invalidate important experimental results. 
In a school laboratory, students can use their smartphones as sensors for various 
experiments, which include analytical chemistry, kinetics and microscopy. 
A suitable app can turn a smartphone into a portable colorimeter or digital 
thermometer. Videc recordings or series of photographs can be used for detailed 
examination of very fast or very slow changes in colour, turbidity or aggregate 
state (e.g. crystal growth) that are difficult to observe in real time. A smartphone 
with a camera can recognize names or CAS numbers of chemicals and display 
various information on their properties, hazards, handling and disposal. 
Databases 
Databases store large amounts of structured information that is easy to search, 
analyse, retrieve and update. Most chemistry-related databases contain 
information on a particular topic, for example: 
» chemical elements (e.g., WebElements, University of Sheffield, UK) 
* physical properties of substances (e.g., Chemspider, Royal Society of 
Chemistry, UK) 
* thermodynamics (e.g., NIST Chemistry WebBook, National Institute of 
Standards and Technology, USA) 
* spectroscopic data (e.g. SDBSWeb, National Institute of Advanced 
Industrial Science and Technology, Japan). 
In most cases, researchers use databases to obtain information on one or 
just a few chemical compounds, but some databases offer advanced tools 
for processing large numbers of entries in order to discover trends and 
correlations between various properties of the studied compounds.

Digital thermometers can measure temperature with more significant figures (or decimal places) than glass bulb thermometers. In contrast to glass bulb thermometers, the accuracy of digital thermometers can be improved by calibration. Finally, digital thermometers typically have better linearity (i.e. their accuracy and precision do not vary significantly across the whole range of measured temperatures).

Electrons (negative charge carriers) move from the anode (negative electrode) to the cathode (positive electrode) through the external circuit (wire, optionally with a voltmeter or other electric device). Cations (positive charge carriers) move from the anode half-cell to the cathode half-cell through the salt bridge. Anions (negative charge carriers) move from the cathode half-cell to the anode half-cell through the salt bridge.
Distillation: excess propan-1-ol is heated with an oxidizing reagent in a distillation apparatus. The vapour of propanal escapes the reaction mixture, passes into the condenser and turns into liquid, which is collected in the receiver flask.
Heating under reflux: propan-1-ol is heated with excess oxidizing reagent in a flask equipped with a reflux condenser. The vapour of the intermediate product (propanal) is continuously returned to the reaction mixture, where it is oxidized further to propanoic acid.
The mixture is spotted on the start line drawn with a pencil and ruler on a piece of chromatographic paper. Pure samples of all three compounds (propan-1-ol, propanal and propanoic acid) are placed as separate spots on the same start line. A sample of  the mixture is also placed as a separate spot on the start line. The paper is dipped into an appropriate solvent in a covered beaker, making sure that the solvent level is below the start line. When the solvent front has moved up most of the paper length, the paper is removed from the beaker, the position of the solvent front is marked with a pencil, and the paper is allowed to dry. The spots are revealed either by spraying the paper with a developing reagent or by placing the paper under UV light. The position of spots  from the mixture can be compared with those from the three pure compounds.
